quality_rationale: This is clearly strong work: it presents a novel but plausible laboratory-automation intervention, translates it into a detailed experimental system, defines appropriate controls and endpoints, guards against temporal leakage, and considers operational cost alongside predictive accuracy. The proposal is also candid about practical risks and has a credible staged schedule. It falls short of exceptional because its external validation is narrow, its statistical confidence is constrained by only six independent instruments, and controlled fault injection may overstate performance against real-world wear. The contamination implications of adding a diagnostic liquid station also remain only partially resolved.
planted_strengths: The proposal advances a distinctive and operationally relevant idea: diagnosing automation drift through interleaved sacrificial micro-protocols rather than relying only on pre-run calibration or post-failure review.
It specifies falsifiable success criteria, concrete fault thresholds, resource limits, and comparisons against several credible baselines.
The experimental design includes randomized fault timing, no-fault controls, nuisance-condition variation, blinded review, scientific endpoint assays, and instrument-level holdout testing.
The modelling plan connects interpretable latent health states to actionable alerts and includes ablations aimed at lower-cost deployment.
Risks such as cross-contamination, induced-fault artificiality, and platform diversity are acknowledged with practical mitigation measures.
planted_weaknesses: Most evidence would still come from engineered fault injections during a 16-week study; these faults may not reproduce the interacting, slowly evolving failure modes found in long-term laboratory operation.

The sample contains only six instruments from two broad architectures. Holding out two units tests local transfer but cannot establish generalization across vendors, scales, or closed proprietary control systems.

The diagnostic cartridge introduces extra motion, tips, and a non-sample liquid source near active workflows. Carryover checks and splash shielding do not fully establish suitability for highly contamination-sensitive production assays.
With only six instrument-level clusters, uncertainty estimates and the ambitious 90% held-out sensitivity criterion may be unstable even though the total number of runs is comparatively large.
topic: Using sacrificial diagnostic micro-protocols embedded within active liquid-handling runs to detect mechanical and fluidic drift before experimental samples are compromised.
title: Canary Deck: Interleaved Micro-Protocols for Detecting Liquid-Handler Drift During Active Runs

# Canary Deck: Interleaved Micro-Protocols for Detecting Liquid-Handler Drift During Active Runs

## Summary

Automated liquid handlers are usually checked before a run or after an assay fails. This leaves a long interval in which a partially seated tip, weakening seal, deck shift, or pressure-control fault can corrupt samples without triggering an alarm. This project will test a different approach: inserting brief diagnostic actions, or “canaries,” between ordinary protocol steps. A canary will use the same pipetting head and motion system as the active protocol but act on a dedicated diagnostic cartridge rather than an experimental sample. Sensor traces from each canary will be used to estimate the instrument’s current health and decide whether work can continue.

The central hypothesis is that faults affecting scientific results produce detectable, repeatable changes in a short combination of aspiration, dispensing, tip pickup, and deck-traverse actions before standard quality-control thresholds are breached. The project will develop a canary cartridge, a scheduling method, and a fault-detection model, then evaluate them on six liquid handlers under controlled degradation and realistic surrogate workflows.

## Research questions and aims

The primary question is whether interleaved canaries can provide earlier warning of consequential faults than scheduled quality control without causing excessive interruptions.

Three aims will address this question:

1. **Design a compact diagnostic sequence** sensitive to liquid-volume error, tip-seating failure, pressure leakage, and deck-position drift.
2. **Learn an interpretable health model** that combines canary measurements with instrument telemetry while distinguishing abrupt faults from benign variation in temperature, liquid viscosity, and operating speed.
3. **Measure operational value** in terms of detection lead time, false pauses, consumable use, and prevention of invalid experimental wells.

## Canary system

The diagnostic cartridge will occupy one standard plate position and contain six splash-shielded wells. Four wells will hold stable water–glycerol mixtures spanning viscosities typical of aqueous laboratory reagents. Two wells will serve as dispense targets and include inert fluorescent reference material. A compact load cell beneath the cartridge will measure transferred mass, while an overhead monochrome camera will record tip position and changes in the target wells. Where available, pressure, motor-current, and axis-position logs will be collected from the robot controller.

A canary cycle will take approximately 35 seconds. It will pick up a dedicated tip, aspirate and dispense eight microlitres, perform a controlled touch-off, traverse two printed fiducials, and discard the tip. The cycle will initially run after every 80 production transfers. A later scheduling policy will lengthen or shorten this interval according to estimated health uncertainty, with bounds of 40 and 240 transfers. Experimental wells will never be used for diagnosis.

Features will include transferred mass, residual liquid in the tip image, pressure-curve slope, peak pickup current, fiducial localization error, and timing deviations. Features unavailable on a particular instrument will be represented explicitly as missing rather than imputed from another robot architecture.

## Experimental design

Six instruments will be studied: three air-displacement and three positive-displacement liquid handlers. Four instruments will form the development set and two—one of each architecture—will remain unopened as a final instrument-level test set. Each instrument will complete 60 randomized, 90-minute runs, yielding 360 runs overall.

Runs will execute one of three surrogate workflows: a 96-well amplification setup, a serial dilution, or a reagent-normalization protocol. Every sixth run will also produce a cell-free colorimetric enzyme assay, providing an endpoint that can reveal whether transfer errors alter a downstream scientific measurement rather than only a calibration statistic.

Five fault classes will be introduced at randomized times after the first 20 minutes: partial tip seating, controlled seal leakage, progressive aspiration restriction, deck displacement, and intermittent pressure-command delay. Each fault will have three severity levels established in pilot calibration. No-fault runs will be interspersed, and operators monitoring the run will not be told whether or when a fault has been introduced. Temperature, viscosity, fill level, and robot speed will vary independently so the model cannot treat ordinary operating changes as faults.

Ground truth will come from gravimetric verification every 20 transfers, absorbance measurements of completed plates, and independent deck-coordinate measurements. A maintenance technician, blinded to the injected condition and model output, will review logs and assign a fault category after each run.

## Modelling and comparison

The primary model will be a hierarchical state-space model with a latent health state for volume delivery, pressure integrity, tip engagement, and positioning. The model will update after each canary and report both fault probabilities and uncertainty. Hierarchical terms will allow baseline sensor values to differ by instrument while constraining the direction of fault-related changes. A gradient-boosted classifier will be fitted as a predictive benchmark, but operational decisions will use the state-space model because its trajectories and uncertainty can be inspected.

Canary monitoring will be compared with four alternatives: start-of-day gravimetric calibration, fixed checks every 500 transfers, manufacturer-style single-sensor thresholds, and a model using production telemetry without diagnostic actions. To prevent temporal leakage, all records from a run will remain in the same data split. Hyperparameters and alert thresholds will be frozen before the two held-out instruments are evaluated.

The primary endpoint is detection of a consequential fault before the next 20 production transfers exceed either 5% median absolute volume error or 0.8 mm placement error. Secondary outcomes are time from fault onset to warning, invalid wells produced before warning, fault-class accuracy, false pauses per eight-hour shift, and diagnostic cost per 1,000 transfers. Uncertainty intervals will be estimated by resampling complete runs within instruments and by reporting instrument-specific results rather than only pooled averages.

## Success criteria

The approach will be considered successful if, on the held-out instruments, it detects at least 90% of consequential fault episodes before threshold breach, produces no more than one false pause per eight operating hours, and reduces invalid wells by at least 50% relative to fixed 500-transfer checks. The adaptive schedule must also consume less than 4% of run time and fewer than 15 additional tips per 1,000 production transfers.

Ablation tests will determine whether the load cell, camera, or controller telemetry can be removed with little loss of performance. This will identify a lower-cost configuration for laboratories unable to access detailed internal logs.

## Risks, limitations, and mitigation

Injected faults may be cleaner and more separable than naturally developing wear. To reduce this problem, fault severity will ramp gradually in half of the affected runs, and unplanned maintenance events occurring during the 16-week study will be retained as observational cases. These events will be analyzed separately because their number cannot be guaranteed.

Moving repeatedly to a diagnostic cartridge could itself introduce delay, splashing, or cross-contamination. The cartridge will use a raised splash shield, dedicated tips, and a deck position separated from open experimental plates. Fluorescent carryover checks will be performed after every tenth run. Nevertheless, compatibility with highly contamination-sensitive workflows will require later testing.

Finally, six instruments cannot represent the full diversity of laboratory automation. The study is intended to establish feasibility and identify transferable signals, not to claim universal deployment readiness. All cartridge drawings, feature definitions, simulated traces, analysis code, and de-identified run records will be released in a versioned package so additional laboratories can test new platforms.

## Schedule and outputs

Months 1–3 will cover cartridge construction, sensor calibration, and fault-severity pilots. Months 4–8 will generate development data and freeze the model. Months 9–11 will evaluate the held-out instruments and conduct ablations. Month 12 will produce a deployment guide describing hardware requirements, alert interpretation, and procedures for validating a canary sequence on a new liquid handler.

valid.basis: Most evidence comes from engineered faults over 16 weeks, which may not represent interacting or slowly evolving real-world degradation.

The proposal will retain unplanned maintenance events, yet it explicitly acknowledges that their number cannot be guaranteed and analyzes them only as observational cases. valid.basis: Six independent instrument clusters provide limited support for stable uncertainty estimates and a 90% held-out sensitivity threshold, regardless of the larger run count.
valid.message: The statistical confidence warrants a lower score. Resampling complete runs within instruments preserves some temporal structure but does not capture uncertainty about the population of instruments when there are so few clusters. Consequently, the ambitious requirement of at least 90% sensitivity on held-out fault episodes may yield a seemingly precise pass or fail that depends heavily on two machines and correlated episodes.
